newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: S&P sees no specific risks in new NZ energy market.
newsitem.headline: S&P sees no specific risks in new NZ energy market.

text.p: Standard and Poor's downgrade of state-owned generator Electricity Corp of New Zealand reflects general uncertainty over the implications of the country's new wholesale electricity market rather than specific risks attached to it, an S&P official said on Monday.
"Our point is the downgrade we've decided on for ECNZ really reflects those changes in the market rather than anything that ECNZ has done," said Louise Griffiths of S&P's Melbourne office.

"A whole range of things could develop that could have an impact on ECNZ...There's no specific concerns that we see, there's nothing that we could highlight as an individual issue that we think's going to cause a risk in the market. It really is an uncertainty about how the various participants will behave," she said in a telephone interview.
S&P earlier said it was cutting ECNZ's long-term credit rating to A+ from AA- and its short-term rating to A-1 from A-1+.
New Zealand will launch its wholesale electricity market on October 1 in the latest stage of deregulation of the industry, setting price on the basis of supply and demand.

Griffiths said the government, as ECNZ's shareholder, afforded protection against debt levels getting too high. On the other hand, any extra cash earned was likely to go towards special dividends rather than debt repayment.
"The dividend policy in effect is going to keep ECNZ's profile fairly stable," Griffiths said.

"No matter how much better they do than their forecasts -- and I think they have a very conservative view of the outcomes in the market and their position in it -- financially they won't be able to take great benefit from improved earnings, it'll be passed through to their shareholder as dividends."

S&P currently awards ratings to three companies in the New Zealand electricity sector. Apart from ECNZ, it rates state-owned national grid operator Trans Power AA+ and Auckland electricity distributor Mercury Energy AA-.

"Those current ratings anticipate various positions within the wholesale market so we wouldn't be out making great changes to ratings as of October 1 because of the wholesale market coming into place. We've known this was coming for a while," Griffiths said.

She said electricity distribution retained a number of monopoly aspects and earnings from the basic "poles and wires" business were seen as very strong. In Trans Power's case, the monopoly element was even greater.
